title: PKCE Flow
description: Secure public client authentication using Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) with OAuth2.

data.text: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) is an extension to the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow. It was originally designed for native applications (mobile apps, desktop apps, single-page applications) that cannot securely store a client secret. PKCE prevents authorization code interception attacks by requiring the client to prove it was the original party that initiated the flow before the authorization server will issue tokens.

In a plain Authorization Code flow, the authorization code is passed through the browser's front channel. An attacker who can intercept the code (via a malicious app registering a custom URL scheme, network eavesdropping, or log injection) can exchange it for tokens. PKCE eliminates this risk: the client generates a random secret (code_verifier) and its transformation (code_challenge) upfront. The authorization server stores the challenge with the code. When the client exchanges the code, it must present the original verifier, which only the legitimate client possesses.

items: code_verifier: A high-entropy random string generated by the client.
code_challenge: BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(code_verifier)) — the transformed value sent to the authorization server.
code_challenge_method: S256 is the only acceptable method. Avoid plain (plaintext) at all costs.
transform: The mathematical operation used to derive the challenge (SHA256 with S256).

data.caption: PKCE Authorization Code Flow with code verifier and challenge
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Client
    participant AuthServer
    participant API
    Client->>Client: Generate code_verifier
    Client->>Client: Generate code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))
    Client->>AuthServer: Redirect with code_challenge, method=S256
    AuthServer->>User: Login & Consent
    User->>AuthServer: Submit credentials
    AuthServer->>Client: Redirect with authorization code
    Client->>AuthServer: POST code + code_verifier to token endpoint
    AuthServer->>AuthServer: Verify SHA256(code_verifier) == code_challenge
    AuthServer->>Client: access_token + refresh_token + id_token
    Client->>API: Request with access_token
    API->>Client: Protected resource

data.title: Never use plain PKCE method
data.text: If code_challenge_method is set to 'plain', the challenge is just the raw verifier in plaintext. An attacker who intercepts the challenge can use it directly as the verifier. Always use S256 (SHA-256 hashing). Most modern authorization servers reject plain challenges from non-legacy clients.

data.text: Step by Step: PKCE in Four Phases

items: At the start of the login flow, generate a code_verifier (random string) and compute code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)). Store verifier locally and pass only the challenge.
Send the user to the authorization endpoint with code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256 instead of (or in addition to) client_id.
After the user authenticates, redirect back with the authorization code. The authorization server will have stored the code_challenge alongside the code.
POST the authorization code AND the original code_verifier to the token endpoint. The server runs SHA256(code_verifier) and compares it to the stored code_challenge. If they match, it issues tokens.

rows: Verifier is hashed before sending; intercepted codes are useless.
Challenge equals the verifier; defeating the protection.

data.title: Where to store the code_verifier
data.text: In a single-page app, store the verifier in memory (not localStorage) to reduce XSS exposure. In a mobile app, use the platform's secure keychain. The verifier must survive the redirect round-trip but should be single-use and short-lived.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: PKCE extends Authorization Code flow for public clients that cannot store a secret
code_verifier is a random secret; code_challenge is its SHA-256 hash
The verifier proves the token exchange request is from the same client that started the flow
Store the verifier in memory or a secure keychain, tied to the session
PKCE is required for mobile apps and strongly recommended for all SPAs
data.takeaway: PKCE turns an interceptable authorization code into a useless string without the matching verifier, closing the main gap in the Authorization Code flow for public clients.
